questions.q: What is the practical difference between authorization and scope in a penetration test?
options: Authorization establishes that testing the client is allowed at all; scope defines precisely which systems and techniques are included
They are two names for exactly the same document with no meaningful difference
Scope is only required for web applications, while authorization covers networks
Authorization is decided by the tester alone; scope must be approved by a court
questions.explain: Authorization answers whether testing the client is permitted at all. Scope is the practical, written detail of exactly which systems, applications, and techniques that authorization actually covers.

questions.q: Why do well-written scoping documents list only what's explicitly in scope, treating everything else as excluded by default?
options: Because out-of-scope items are illegal to write down in a contract
Because clients prefer shorter documents regardless of completeness
Because listing exclusions instead would require a government permit
It protects the tester from disputes over systems that were never explicitly authorized, and protects the client from unintended testing
questions.explain: Default-exclude scoping means anything not explicitly named is out of bounds, preventing arguments like 'you didn't say we couldn't touch that' after the fact.

questions.q: During a scan of an in-scope subnet, a tester discovers a server that is reachable but was never named in the scope document. What should the tester do?
options: Exploit it immediately since it was reachable from an in-scope system
Ignore it entirely and never mention it to the client
Document what was observed from outside it, then get a written scope amendment from the client before testing it further
Ask a colleague informally whether it seems like it should be in scope
questions.explain: Testing a system not named in scope — even if reachable — is the same unauthorized-access problem covered in Lesson 1. The correct step is to pause, document the observation, and get a written scope amendment first.

questions.q: Why does scoping typically call out cloud and third-party-hosted assets as their own category of question?
options: Cloud assets never need to be scoped since they're always considered in scope automatically
A client's authorization for their application layer doesn't automatically cover the underlying cloud provider's infrastructure, which has its own acceptable-use policy
Cloud providers prohibit all penetration testing under any circumstances
Third-party systems are always out of scope and never require discussion
questions.explain: Providers like AWS and Azure publish their own acceptable-use policies governing security testing against their infrastructure, so scope has to address whether authorization extends beyond the client's own application layer.

questions.q: Which of the following typically requires its own explicit, separate sign-off beyond the standard technical scope?
options: Testing the in-scope production web application listed by hostname
Scanning the exact IP range named in the scope document
Social engineering of specific named employees or physical office premises
Reviewing the escalation procedure listed in the Rules of Engagement
questions.explain: Social engineering against named individuals or physical premises raises distinct legal and HR considerations, so it typically needs its own explicit authorization separate from the general technical scope.
